title: The Concept of Money Supply
outcomes: Define money supply and the "public", explain why money supply is measured, and identify its sources — the central bank (high-powered money) and commercial banks (credit money); explain CBDC and the status of crypto-currencies.
Compute the RBI's measures M1, M2, M3 and M4 and currency with the public.

Explain the money multiplier and its determinants (currency ratio, reserve ratio, excess reserves), and compute it with m = (1 + c)/(r + e + c); distinguish it from the credit (deposit) multiplier 1/r.
Explain how open market operations and government borrowing from the RBI (WMA/overdraft) change money supply.

meta.exam_tip: Memorise M1–M4 exactly (M2 and M4 add POST OFFICE deposits; M3 adds TIME deposits of banks). For numericals: m = (1 + c)/(r + e + c); credit multiplier = 1/r. Every ratio — c, r, e — moves inversely with the multiplier.

concepts.title: Introduction — money supply and who the "public" is
body: Whatever its form, money is a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. For policy, money is the set of liquid financial assets whose changes can affect overall economic activity. Stability needs money supply kept at an optimum level — which requires measuring it accurately and regulating it.

Money supply refers to money held by the public. The "public" means all economic units — households, firms, institutions, local authorities, non-bank financial companies, non-departmental public undertakings, foreign central banks and governments, and the IMF's deposits with the RBI — EXCEPT the producers of money: the government (Centre, States, local bodies in this context) and the banking system (RBI and banks accepting demand deposits).
So inter-bank deposits and money held by the government and banks are excluded.

Broad money (M3) in international usage covers currency, deposits with agreed maturity up to two years, deposits redeemable at notice up to three months, repos, money-market fund units and debt securities up to two years.
concepts.analogy: Money supply counts the water in people's buckets, not the water still in the municipal tank (the RBI and banks) or in the government's own drums.
concepts.work: Bank treasury and economics teams track the RBI's fortnightly money-supply data to anticipate liquidity and interest-rate moves.

concepts.title: Rationale of measuring money supply
body: (1) Analysis: it helps understand the causes of money growth.

(2) Policy: it tells whether the money stock is consistent with price stability, and why it deviates. Central banks stabilise prices and GDP growth by managing the monetary base; the success of monetary policy depends on how controllable the monetary base and money supply are.
concepts.analogy: You cannot regulate the water level of a dam without a gauge — measuring money supply is the gauge.
concepts.work: Economists use money growth as one input when forecasting inflation and RBI policy decisions for clients.

concepts.title: Sources of money supply; CBDC and crypto-currencies
body: Money supply depends on (a) the central bank's decisions under its legal authority and (b) the response of commercial banks to the central bank's policy changes.

Currency is issued only by the sovereign or the central bank on its behalf, and is legal tender. Paper currency is representative money — a debt instrument: a liability of the central bank (and government) and an asset of the public. The central bank is the primary source of money; the high-powered money it issues is the base for all other money. Its fiat money is backed by reserves and guaranteed by the government.

In principle currency should be backed by assets (gold, foreign exchange); in practice most countries use a minimum reserve system — the central bank may issue any amount of currency while holding only a prescribed minimum of gold and foreign assets as backing.
The second source is commercial banks: they create credit money through lending and borrowing with the public. High-powered money plus credit money make up the common measure of money stock.

Money has evolved from commodity to metallic to paper to digital. A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is legal tender issued by a central bank in digital form — like sovereign currency, exchangeable at par, a medium of payment and safe store of value, and a liability of the central bank. The RBI is introducing the Digital Rupee (e₹) in phases through pilots.

Crypto-currencies are not legally recognised as currency in India and are not counted as money. The RBI has clarified that banks cannot rely on its 2018 circular (which barred dealing in virtual currencies) — that circular was set aside.
concepts.analogy: The RBI pours the first jug of water (high-powered money); banks keep passing part of it from glass to glass, so the total water people can drink is many times the jug.
concepts.work: Banks' finance teams must classify CBDC holdings and understand that crypto assets are not "cash or cash equivalents" for accounting or regulatory purposes in India.

concepts.title: Measurement of money supply — M1, M2, M3, M4
body: Many forms of credit money make measurement hard, and measures differ by country, time and purpose. The RBI has compiled monetary statistics since July 1935. Until 1967-68 it published only narrow money M1 (currency + demand deposits with the public). From 1967-68 it added "aggregate monetary resources" (AMR). From April 1977, on the Second Working Group's recommendations, it publishes four measures plus reserve money.
M1 = currency notes and coins with the public + demand deposits with the banking system (current accounts and savings accounts) + other deposits with the RBI.
M2 = M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks.
M3 = M1 + time deposits with the banking system. M3 is "broad money" and the most widely used measure.
M4 = M3 + total deposits with the Post Office Savings Organisation (excluding National Savings Certificates).
Liquidity falls from M1 to M4: M1 is the most liquid. Currency with the public = notes in circulation + rupee coins + small coins − cash on hand with banks.
Reserve money (monetary base, high-powered money) = currency in circulation + other deposits with the RBI + balances that banks hold with the RBI.

blocks.title: RBI measures of money supply

concepts.analogy: M1 is cash in hand plus money in your current account; M3 adds your fixed deposits; M2 and M4 add post office savings.
concepts.work: Bank auditors verify the "demand" and "time" liability classification banks report to the RBI, because those numbers feed M1 and M3 and also determine CRR/SLR.

concepts.title: Determinants of money supply and the money multiplier concept
body: Two views: money supply is exogenous (fixed by the central bank) or endogenous (driven by economic activity, people's currency preferences, interest rates). Current practice uses the money-multiplier approach, linking money stock to the monetary base (currency in circulation + bank reserves); total money supply is jointly determined by the central bank, commercial banks and the public.
The RBI creates the monetary base (high-powered money, H). Banks lend out excess reserves, creating deposits, so a one-rupee rise in H raises money supply by more than one rupee.

M = C + D (currency with the public + deposits). M = m × H, so the money multiplier m = money supply ÷ monetary base. Example: if a ₹100 crore open market purchase finally adds ₹400 crore to money supply, m = 4.

Simplest case (banks hold no excess reserves and the public holds no currency): m = 1/R, where R is the reserve ratio. At R = 10%, m = 10; at R = 5%, m = 20. Higher reserve ratio → smaller multiplier.
Money that leaks into currency is not multiplied; only the part that supports deposits is. So holding more cash shrinks the multiplier.
concepts.analogy: High-powered money is the seed; the money multiplier is how many plants grow from it. Seeds kept in the pocket (currency) never sprout.
concepts.work: Treasury analysts estimate how much a CRR change will release or absorb — a direct multiplier calculation.

concepts.title: The money multiplier approach (Friedman and Schwartz)
body: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz (1963) named three proximate determinants: (a) the stock of high-powered money H — behaviour of the central bank; (b) the reserve ratio r = reserves/deposits — behaviour of commercial banks; (c) the currency–deposit ratio c = C/D — behaviour of the public.
Central bank: with public and bank behaviour unchanged, money supply varies directly with H.

Commercial banks: a higher required reserve ratio forces banks to contract loans and deposits — money supply falls; a lower one expands it. Banks often hold excess reserves (ER = total reserves − required reserves) as a buffer. The excess reserve ratio e falls when market interest rates rise (higher opportunity cost of idle reserves) and rises when banks fear larger deposit withdrawals. In crises banks may refuse to lend to small firms even when policy rates are cut, slowing money growth despite easy policy (e.g. banks parked huge sums in the RBI's reverse repo window during COVID-19 despite a low 3.35% rate).

Public: when deposits are converted into currency, less credit can be created — m and money supply are inversely related to c. The currency ratio reflects banking habits, and falls with financial development, easier access, new liquid assets and innovation. A higher time-deposit to demand-deposit ratio frees reserves and enlarges deposit expansion.
Derivation: M = C + D and H = C + Reserves. With c = C/D and r = Reserves/D: M = (1 + c)D and H = (c + r)D, so m = (1 + c)/(r + c) and M = m × H. With excess reserves: m = (1 + c)/(r + e + c).
m is a function of c (set by depositors), e (set by banks) and r (set by the central bank through CRR and settlement needs). The lower these ratios, the larger the multiplier.
concepts.analogy: Each ratio is a leak in a pipe: the more water leaks out as cash (c) or is held back in tanks (r, e), the less reaches the end of the pipe.
concepts.work: Bank ALM committees decide how much excess liquidity to hold; collectively these decisions change e and the economy-wide multiplier.

concepts.title: Credit multiplier and its difference from the money multiplier
body: The credit (deposit) multiplier shows how much additional deposit money the banking system creates by lending reserves above the requirement. Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ required reserve ratio. At 20%, it is 5.

It results from fractional-reserve banking: when a bank lends part of a deposit, the borrower gets a new deposit while the original depositor keeps his claim — the bank has more liabilities than cash. Example with a 10% ratio: an initial deposit of ₹1,000 supports loans of ₹900, then ₹810, ₹729 and so on, until total deposits reach 1,000 × 1/0.10 = ₹10,000.
Money created by banks is no different from money issued by the central bank, but creating money is not the same as creating wealth.
The two multipliers differ because banks usually hold more than the minimum reserves, and borrowers convert part of their loans into cash. So the actual money multiplier is smaller than 1/r.
concepts.analogy: A rumour passed along a chain — each person repeats 90% of what they heard; the total words spoken add up to ten times the original sentence.
concepts.work: Credit-growth projections for banks start from deposits and the reserve requirement — a practical credit multiplier exercise.

concepts.title: Monetary policy, government expenditure and money supply
body: To stimulate activity the central bank injects liquidity, e.g. through an open market purchase of government securities, which adds to banks' reserves (monetary base). If banks hold no excess reserves, people do not hold extra currency and borrowers want loans, ΔMoney supply = (1/R) × ΔReserves.

An open market sale works the other way — it drains reserves and reduces money supply. (Exam note: one sentence of the study material, as printed, says an open market purchase reduces reserves; that is a slip — the material's own preceding sentences, and standard theory, show that a purchase injects reserves and a sale withdraws them. Answer on that basis.)
Can the multiplier be zero? Yes — if interest rates are very low and banks simply hold new reserves as risk-free excess reserves, nothing is lent out.

Government expenditure: when Central or State cash balances fall below the minimum, they can use the RBI's Ways and Means Advances (WMA) or overdraft. When the government spends this money, its account with the RBI is debited and the recipient's account in a commercial bank (say a government employee's salary account) is credited — banks' balances with the RBI rise. These excess reserves can expand money supply through the multiplier.
concepts.analogy: An open market purchase is the RBI buying bonds from banks with freshly created money — like topping up every bank's tank so more water can flow out as loans.
concepts.work: Liquidity forecasting desks in banks track government cash balances with the RBI, because government spending from WMA adds reserves to the banking system.

illustrations.title: Computing M1, M2, M3 and M4
illustrations.q: Data (₹ crore): currency with the public 3,20,000; demand deposits with banks 2,80,000; other deposits with RBI 6,000; savings deposits with post office savings banks 18,000; time deposits with banks 14,50,000; total post office deposits excluding NSC 62,000. Compute M1 to M4.

solution.text: M2 and M3 are both built on M1, not on each other. M4 adds the total post office deposits to M3.

illustrations.title: Currency with the public
illustrations.q: Notes in circulation ₹33,40,000 crore; rupee coins ₹31,200 crore; small coins ₹750 crore; cash on hand with banks ₹1,18,000 crore. Find currency with the public.

solution.text: Currency with the public = 33,40,000 + 31,200 + 750 − 1,18,000 = ₹32,53,950 crore. Cash held by banks is excluded because banks are producers of money, not part of the "public".

illustrations.title: The money multiplier with currency and excess reserves
illustrations.q: Required reserve ratio r = 8%, excess reserve ratio e = 2%, currency–deposit ratio c = 0.30; high-powered money H = ₹60,000 crore. Find m and M. What happens to m if (a) r rises to 13%, (b) c falls to 0.20? Compare with the simple multiplier.

solution.text: (a) r = 13%: m = 1.30 ÷ 0.45 = 2.89 — a higher reserve ratio lowers the multiplier.
(b) c = 0.20: m = 1.20 ÷ 0.30 = 4 — less cash holding raises the multiplier.
Simple multiplier 1/r = 1/0.08 = 12.5; the actual multiplier is much smaller because of currency drain and excess reserves.

illustrations.title: Credit creation by the banking system
illustrations.q: A fresh deposit of ₹2,00,000 is made. Required reserve ratio is 8%. Show the first rounds of deposit creation and the total; repeat the total for a 20% ratio.

illustrations.title: Open market purchase
illustrations.q: The RBI buys government securities worth ₹5,000 crore from banks. Reserve ratio is 10%. Find the rise in money supply (a) if there is no currency drain or excess reserves, (b) if the public holds currency equal to 25% of deposits.

solution.text: (b) m = 1.25 ÷ 0.35 = 3.57; ΔM = 5,000 × 1.25 ÷ 0.35 ≈ ₹17,857 crore (using the rounded multiplier 3.57 gives about ₹17,850 crore). Currency drain sharply reduces the expansion.

checks.label: money created with currency drain (exact multiplier 1.25/0.35)

jobs.title: Explaining a CRR cut to a board
jobs.role: CA as CFO of a small finance bank
jobs.situation: The RBI cuts CRR by 0.5 percentage points.
steps: Compute reserves released = 0.5% × net demand and time liabilities.
Explain that the system-wide money multiplier rises as r falls.
Plan deployment — loans if demand exists, otherwise investments (excess reserves raise e and blunt the effect).
jobs.takeaway: A CRR change acts directly on the reserve ratio in the money multiplier.
jobs.think: Why might money supply not rise much after the cut?
jobs.answer: If loan demand is weak or banks are risk-averse, they hold the released funds as excess reserves (higher e), so the multiplier barely changes.

jobs.title: Verifying a bank's demand and time liabilities
jobs.role: Articled assistant on a bank branch audit
jobs.situation: You must check the branch's return of demand and time liabilities.
steps: Classify current accounts and the demand portion of savings as demand liabilities; fixed deposits as time liabilities.
Note that misclassification distorts CRR/SLR and national M1/M3 statistics.
jobs.takeaway: The building blocks of M1 and M3 come from millions of bank returns like this one.

jobs.title: Client asks: is crypto money?
jobs.situation: A client holding crypto assets calls them "cash" in his books.
steps: Explain crypto-currencies are not legal tender in India and are not counted as money.
Explain the Digital Rupee (CBDC) is legal tender issued by the RBI.
Reclassify crypto holdings as investments/virtual digital assets as per applicable law.
jobs.takeaway: Legal tender status decides what counts as money.

mcqs.q: For measuring money supply, the "public" excludes:
options: The government and the banking system
mcqs.explain: Producers of money — government and banks — are excluded.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is part of the "public" for money-supply purposes?
options: Foreign central banks holding deposits with the RBI
mcqs.explain: Foreign central banks, governments and the IMF's deposits with the RBI count as public.

mcqs.q: Which institution is the basic (primary) source of money supply in every country?
mcqs.explain: The central bank issues high-powered money — the base for all other money.

mcqs.q: Money created by commercial banks through lending is called:
mcqs.explain: Banks create deposits as they lend.

mcqs.q: Under the minimum reserve system, the central bank:
options: May issue any amount of currency while holding a prescribed minimum of gold and foreign assets
Must back every note fully with gold
Cannot issue currency without Parliament's approval for each note
Issues currency only against government deficits
mcqs.explain: Most countries follow this system.

mcqs.q: A CBDC is:
options: Legal tender issued by a central bank in digital form
mcqs.explain: India's CBDC is the Digital Rupee (e₹), a liability of the RBI.

mcqs.q: In India, crypto-currencies are:
options: Not legally recognised as currency and not counted as money
mcqs.explain: They face legal uncertainty and are not money.

mcqs.q: M1 consists of:
options: Currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with the RBI
mcqs.explain: Narrow money M1.

mcqs.q: M3 equals:
options: M1 + time deposits with the banking system
mcqs.explain: M3 builds on M1, not on M2.

mcqs.q: M2 equals:
options: M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks
mcqs.explain: M2 adds post office savings bank deposits.

mcqs.q: Which measure is called broad money?
mcqs.explain: M3 is broad money and most widely used.

mcqs.q: The RBI began publishing four measures of money supply (M1 to M4) from:
mcqs.explain: Following the Second Working Group on Money Supply.

mcqs.q: Currency with the public 3,20,000; demand deposits 2,80,000; other deposits with RBI 6,000; time deposits 14,50,000 (₹ crore). M3 is:
mcqs.explain: M1 = 6,06,000; M3 = 6,06,000 + 14,50,000 = 20,56,000. ₹20,50,000 omits other deposits with RBI; ₹17,70,000 omits demand deposits.

mcqs.q: Notes in circulation 33,40,000; rupee coins 31,200; small coins 750; cash with banks 1,18,000 (₹ crore). Currency with the public is:
mcqs.explain: Add notes and coins, subtract cash held by banks: 33,71,950 − 1,18,000 = 32,53,950.

mcqs.q: If R = 10% and there is no currency drain or excess reserves, the money multiplier is:
A ₹100 crore open market purchase finally raises money supply by ₹400 crore. The money multiplier is:
The money-multiplier approach identifying H, r and c as proximate determinants was given by:
mcqs.explain: Friedman and Schwartz (1963).

mcqs.q: The currency–deposit ratio reflects the behaviour of:
mcqs.explain: c = C/D shows banking habits of people.

mcqs.q: The money multiplier is NEGATIVELY related to:
options: The currency ratio, the reserve ratio and the excess reserve ratio
mcqs.explain: Higher c, r or e means less deposit expansion.

mcqs.q: With r = 0.08, e = 0.02 and c = 0.30, the money multiplier m = (1 + c)/(r + e + c) is:
mcqs.explain: 1.30/0.40 = 3.25. 12.5 is the simple multiplier 1/r; 4.33 (= 1.30/0.30) wrongly leaves r and e out of the denominator; 2.5 uses 1/0.40.

mcqs.q: Excess reserves of banks tend to FALL when:
mcqs.explain: Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of idle reserves.

mcqs.q: Total reserves are ₹800 billion and required reserves ₹650 billion. Excess reserves are:
If the required reserve ratio is 12.5%, the credit multiplier is:
A fresh deposit of ₹2,00,000 with a 20% reserve ratio can support total deposits of:
mcqs.explain: 2,00,000 × 1/0.2 = 10,00,000. ₹8,00,000 is the new credit only (excluding the initial deposit).

mcqs.q: The money multiplier is usually smaller than the credit multiplier because:
options: Banks hold excess reserves and borrowers convert part of loans into cash
The RBI prints too much money
mcqs.explain: Both leakages reduce deposit expansion.

mcqs.q: An open market SALE of securities by the RBI will:
options: Reduce bank reserves and money supply
Increase bank reserves and money supply
mcqs.explain: Banks pay for the securities from their reserves.

mcqs.q: The money multiplier could be close to zero when:
options: Interest rates are very low and banks hold new reserves as excess reserves
mcqs.explain: If banks do not lend, no deposits are created.

mcqs.q: When the government spends money borrowed from the RBI under WMA/overdraft:
options: Banks' reserves with the RBI rise and money supply can expand
There is no effect on money supply
mcqs.explain: The government account is debited; recipients' bank accounts are credited, adding reserves.

questions.q: From the data (₹ crore) compute M1, M2, M3 and M4: currency with the public 2,40,000; demand deposits with banks 4,10,000; other deposits with RBI 9,000; post office savings bank deposits 35,000; time deposits with banks 18,20,000; total post office deposits (excluding NSC) 1,20,000.
remarks: The classic error is building M3 on M2.
mistakes: Adding post office deposits to M3.
Leaving out other deposits with the RBI.
tips: Write each definition before the numbers.

questions.q: Required reserve ratio 10%; currency ₹500 billion; demand deposits ₹1,000 billion; excess reserves ₹5 billion. Find (a) c and e, (b) money supply, (c) the money multiplier, (d) the multiplier if the reserve ratio rises to 15%, (e) the simple deposit multiplier. Comment.

model.text: (e) Simple multiplier = 1/0.1 = 10. The actual multiplier is far smaller because half of people's money is held as currency, which is not multiplied; a higher reserve ratio lowers it further.

remarks: Show the formula with symbols first.

checks.label: e as a percentage of deposits (e = 0.005)

questions.q: The required reserve ratio is 12.5%. (a) Find the credit multiplier. (b) What total deposits can a fresh deposit of ₹5,00,000 support, and how much new credit is created? (c) If the RBI buys securities worth ₹2,000 crore from banks, what is the maximum rise in money supply? State the assumptions.

model.text: Assumptions: banks keep no excess reserves, the public holds no extra currency, and there is enough demand for loans.

remarks: Distinguish total deposits from new credit.
mistakes: Treating an OMO purchase as reducing money supply.
tips: List the assumptions — they explain why reality differs.

summary: Money supply = money held by the public (excludes government and banking system).
Measured to understand money growth and to guide monetary policy.
Sources: central bank (high-powered money, fiat, minimum reserve system) and banks (credit money). CBDC (e₹) is legal tender; crypto is not money in India.
M1 = C + DD + other deposits with RBI; M2 = M1 + PO savings deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits (broad money); M4 = M3 + total PO deposits (excl. NSC). Four measures since April 1977.
Money multiplier m = M/H = (1 + c)/(r + e + c); simple 1/r. Friedman–Schwartz: H (central bank), r (banks/central bank), c (public).
Credit multiplier = 1/required reserve ratio; larger than the actual money multiplier because of excess reserves and cash drain.
OMO purchase raises reserves and money supply; sale reduces them. Government spending from WMA/OD adds bank reserves.
remember: Currency with public = notes + rupee coins + small coins − cash with banks.
Excess reserves = total reserves − required reserves.
traps: M3 is built on M1, not M2.
Higher c, r or e → LOWER multiplier.
Cash held by banks is not currency with the public.

viva.q: Who determines the money supply according to the money multiplier approach?
viva.model: According to Friedman and Schwartz, money supply is jointly determined by the central bank, which controls high-powered money; the commercial banks, through the reserve ratio and excess reserves they keep; and the public, through the currency–deposit ratio, that is how much cash people hold compared with deposits.

points.pt: Commercial banks — reserve / excess reserve ratio

viva.q: What is the money multiplier, and how do the currency ratio and the reserve ratio affect it?
viva.model: The money multiplier is the ratio of money supply to high-powered money, so it shows how much money supply rises for each rupee of monetary base; it equals one plus c divided by r plus e plus c. A higher currency ratio lowers the multiplier because cash is not multiplied, and a higher reserve ratio also lowers it because banks can lend less.

viva.q: What is the credit multiplier and why is it larger than the actual money multiplier?
viva.model: The credit multiplier is one divided by the required reserve ratio; it shows how many times the banking system can expand an initial deposit through repeated lending under fractional reserve banking. The actual money multiplier is smaller because banks keep excess reserves above the minimum and borrowers hold part of their loans as cash.

viva.q: How does government expenditure financed by Ways and Means Advances affect money supply?
viva.model: When the government's cash falls short it borrows from the RBI through Ways and Means Advances or overdraft. When it spends, its account with the RBI is debited and the recipients' accounts in commercial banks are credited, so banks' reserves with the RBI rise. These excess reserves can increase money supply through the multiplier process.
